entries.title: Berlin: 1 dead, 16 injured after car ramming at CSD Pride event
entries.summary: A citywide manhunt is underway after a van drove into a crowd during Pride celebrations, known locally as Christopher Street Day (CSD). Police have identified a suspect tied to Berlin's "Islamist scene."
entries.content:
Germany

Berlin: 1 dead, 16 injured in car ramming at CSD Pride event

Published July 25, 2026last updated July 26, 2026

A citywide manhunt is underway after a van drove into a crowd during Pride celebrations, known locally as Christopher Street Day (CSD). Police have identified a suspect tied to Berlin's "Islamist scene."

What you need to know

  • 1 person was killed and 3 people suffered life-threatening injuries after a car drove into a crowd at one of Europe's biggest LGBTQ+ Pride events
  • Police have identified a suspect associated with 'the Islamist scene in Berlin'
  • No arrests have been made, but a manhunt has been launched and more than 2,200 personnel have been deployed as part of the police operation
  • The area around Tiergarten in central Berlin remains closed off

At least one person has died and 16 people were injured, "some seriously", police said, after a vehicle was driven into a crowd near Berlin's annual Pride event, Christopher Street Day (CSD) on Saturday night.

"We believe that a vehicle entered the Tiergarten park and hit several people," police said on social media.

Berlin's CSD is one of Europe's biggest Pride events celebrating the LGBTQ+ community. It attracts tens of thousands of visitors from around the world each year.

What do we know about the incident at the Berlin CSD event?

Police spokesperson Florian Nath said a suspect has been identified who was known to police and "is believed to be associated with the Islamist scene in Berlin."

It was unclear whether there were other perpetrators. No arrests have been made yet.

Three of the 16 injured had suffered "life-threatening injuries," Nath told reporters at the scene.

He added that more than 2,200 personnel were involved in the police response, including officers from Hamburg and other federal states.

The vehicle in question is a white minivan or compact SUV, he said.

DW reporters on the scene in Berlin said police officers armed with machine guns were patrolling the streets of the German capital.

Police said early on Sunday morning that the Tiergarten remained closed off.

"We are now piecing together the facts based on the evidence found at the scene. The search radius covers the entire city," Nath said. "We need to use daylight tomorrow to meticulously examine the evidence."

Berlin mayor, Chancellor Merz condemn 'horrific' act

Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner, who visited the scene, described the incident as "an attack on our free and open society."

"After a peaceful and colorful CSD, the assembly for a tolerant and peaceful Berlin was attacked in the most brutal way. Berlin is the city of freedom, and our freedom has been attacked in the most horrific way today," he said on X.

In remarks to reporters at the scene, Wegner said, "We will not allow our way of life and our way of living together to be taken from us."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz also condemned what he called a "horrific act."

In a statement, Merz said he and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt would ensure "this horrific act is fully investigated and punished."

Pride parade participants told to 'go home, please'

Hundreds of thousands of people had taken to the streets of Berlin on Saturday to advocate for tolerance and diversity, culminating in concerts at the Brandenburg Gate.

The event was called off around 10:15 p.m., and a band's performance was interrupted. Authorities urged people to "go home, please," and avoid routes through Tiergarten.

The CSD parade ended on 17 June Street, which crosses Berlin's Tiergarten to the Brandenburg Gate. The Gate has been the venue for concerts since Friday.

Berlin's CSD was first held in 1979, making it Germany's oldest Pride event. Its name comes from Christopher Street — the site of the 1969 Stonewall riots in New York City.

CSD has since evolved from a small protest into a major fixture of the city's cultural and political calendar.

Germany's history of car rammings

Germany has seen a number of car rammings at major public events in recent years.

In 2016, a Tunisian-born man drove a truck into a Christmas market in Berlin, killing 12 people, in the deadliest Islamist attack in Germany's postwar history.

In 2024, a man plowed his car into a busy Christmas market in the city of Magdeburg, killing at least two people and injuring more than 60. The perpetrator was a Saudi-born atheist who held anti-Islamic and far-right beliefs.

Earlier this year, two people were killed after a man drove a car through a crowd in the eastern German city of Leipzig. Investigators treated the incident as a rampage and the suspect, a German national, was remanded to a psychiatric hospital.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: WAFCON 2026: What you need to know
entries.summary: Several months after it was supposed to start and with more teams than first planned, WAFCON 2026 is finally set to begin. The hosts want a maiden title while a tournament outsider have one of its best players.
entries.content:
Morocco

WAFCON 2026: What you need to know

July 25, 2026

Several months after it was supposed to start and with more teams than first planned, WAFCON 2026 is finally set to begin. The hosts want a maiden title while a tournament outsider have one of its best players.

What is WAFCON?

The Women's Africa  Cup of Nations is the continental tournament to find the best women's international team in Africa. It has existed in some form since 1991 but the current competition's history really starts in 1998; it has generally been held every two years since then.

Holders Nigeria have won a record 10 titles with only Equatorial Guinea (2012 as hosts) and South Africa (2022) having broken their domination of the tournament.

Originally planned as a 12-team tournament, the African football federation (CAF) added four more teams after qualification. Those four sides had all lost out in the second phase of qualifying but were then reinstated despite CAF earlier denying such changes were afoot. It was a sign of things to come.

Where and when is WAFCON 2026 being played?

For a third successive tournament, WAFCON is to be hosted by Morocco. Specifically, games are to be played in Rabat and Casablanca with a a third city, Fez, dropped from the initial lineup when the fixtures were announced.

Since pulling out of hosting the men's AFCON in 2015, Morocco has become the favored African destination for both CAF and global football's governors FIFA. The North African country, which also hosted the men's AFCON last year, is to cohost the 2030 men's World Cup and has been chosen, or been the sole bidder, for a number of continental and international youth tournaments.

The tournament opener, between Algeria and Senegal, is on July 26, with Morocco opening against Kenya later that day. The final is scheduled for August 16 in Rabat.

Why is WAFCON being played straight after the men's World Cup?

It wasn't supposed to be. After weeks of rumor, denial and a South African offer to step in as hosts, CAF announced just 12 days before the tournament was due to start in March that it would be postponed. CAF, rather vaguely, cited "unforeseen circumstances" as the reason for the delay.

"It is a combination of factors, and it is not a decision taken lightly," Luxolo September, CAF's head of communications, told DW at the time.

"There is a question of the host nation, Morocco, requesting a postponement for a number of reasons. There has been a lot of interaction between Morocco, FIFA and CAF regarding the date. This is not a nice position for us. We have taken no joy from this. We would have loved to play in this window. It is a window we had requested."

Many teams, fans and players were frustrated by the short notice, with preparations made and money shelled out far in advance. It was not the first time though. Two years earlier, the tournament had been postponed by a year because the tournament clashed with the Olympics in Paris — a key date in the women's football calendar.

As well as coming hot on the heels of the men's World Cup, WAFCON 26 will now finish as the season starts in many countries. Germany's women's season for example, kicks off with the first round of the DFB Cup on same weekend as the WAFCON final.

Who are the favorites at WAFCON 26?

Hosts Morocco will want to match their men's side, who won their AFCON tournament in controversial circumstances earlier this year, their maiden title, having lost the previous two finals.

Perennial champions Nigeria will once again enter as favorites while the 2022 winners, South Africa, will also fancy their chances. Below that are a host of teams who could cause a few surprises, including Ivory Coast, Egypt and debutants Cape Verde, whose men's side became one of the stories of the World Cup.

Who are the players to watch at WAFCON 26?

Apart from Zambia's Barbra Banda and Racheal Kundananji, Nigeria's Rasheedat Ajibade may be the most highly regarded talent. Named player of the tournament in 2024, Ajibade is a leader for her team, as well as its sharpest attacking threat. At the other end of the pitch, Nigeria will rely on Chiamaka Nnadozie, regarded as the continent's best goalkeeper.

Hosts Morocco will look to Ghizlaine Chebbak. The top scorer at the last two tournaments, 35-year-old Chebbak may not have too many better chances to win a first major international honor.

Elsewhere, Tabitha Chawinga, of French champions Lyon, will carry the hopes of debutants Malawi, the lowest FIFA-ranked side in the competition. Chawinga's international career has been interrupted by her club commitments but she has an exceptional 25 goals in her 11 caps to date. Her sister, Temwa, is also in the Malawi squad and plays her club football for the Kansas City Current of the NWSL, the top league in the United States. There, she won the 2025 Golden Boot as top goal scorer with 15 goals in 23 games.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

entries.title: Flavio Bolsonaro gets party nod to run against Brazil's Lula
entries.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro won support from Argentine President Javier Milei and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though tariffs imposed by Donald Trump's administration could complicate his path to the presidency.
entries.content:
Brazil

Flavio Bolsonaro gets party nod to run against Brazil's Lula

July 25, 2026

Flavio Bolsonaro won support from Argentine President Javier Milei and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though tariffs imposed by Donald Trump's administration could complicate his path to the presidency.

Flavio Bolsonaro, son of Brazil's former President Jair Bolsonaro, was confirmed Saturday as his father's Liberal Party candidate to challenge incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.

"Bolsonaro's blood flows here," he declared at the party convention in Sao Paulo.

His father has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his loss to Lula in the 2022 election.

Brazil's presidential election is scheduled to be held on October 4. If no candidate wins an outright majority, a runoff will take place on October 25.

Support from Milei and Netanyahu

The younger Bolsonaro still lacks a running mate and centrist backing, while the absence of major political figures at Saturday's party convention highlighted his struggle to build an anti-Lula alliance before October.

He did, however, get support from Argentine President Javier Milei, who endorsed his bid for the presidency.

"I firmly believe there is no one else capable of putting an end to the Lula risk hanging over Brazil," Milei, who attended the party convention, said.

Bolsonaro also showed a short video message of support from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Bolsonaro's campaign faces challenges

He has also developed ties with US conservatives and Donald Trump's administration. In May, he posted pictures he took in the Oval Office with the US president on social media.

The Trump administration has, however, since imposed new tariffs on Brazilian exports of up to 37.5%.

A poll released Friday shows Lula would defeat Flavio Bolsonaro in a potential runoff, 48% to 43%. A June survey showed Lula ahead 47% to 43%.

Lula's left-wing Workers' Party (PT) is expected to formally nominate him as its candidate in August.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Serbia's LGBTQ+ community faces 'epidemic of violence'
entries.summary: Documented cases of violence against LGBTQ+ people in Serbia have never been higher. The attacks are part of a larger shift in society targeting marginalized people.
entries.content:
Serbia

Serbia's LGBTQ+ community faces 'epidemic of violence'

July 25, 2026

Documented cases of violence against LGBTQ+ people in Serbia have never been higher. The attacks are part of a larger shift in society targeting marginalized people.

Amid a slew of blows and homophobic insults, the woman on the bus lashed out at Aleksandar Savic and stabbed him with a sharp object. Later, in the emergency room, doctors treated Savic for a cut to the calf and injuries to his eye.

Incidents like the July 11 attack on Savic — also know as drag queen Alexis Plastik — don't happen often in Belgrade. But violence against people who don't look or act like the mainstream in the EU candidate country is becoming increasingly common.

Just a few hours earlier, Vladimir Arsenijevic, author and program director of the annual Krokodil Literary Festival, was attacked in central Belgrade in the middle of the day by right-wing thugs, as he was preparing for a memorial event commemorating the 1995 Srebrenica genocide.

Speaking with broadcaster N1, Plastik called out the "epidemic of violence" in Serbia. The increasing violence by groups associated with President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, has reinforced the feeling among many people that anyone who is different can become a target, and that no one is safe.

"Violence is becoming increasingly normal, while protection against it is anything but guaranteed — especially for those who speak out against social or political problems, or who are unpopular with the general public," said Matija Stefanovic, the program coordinator for the LGBTQ+ group Da se Zna! ("For Your Information!"), which documents violence against queer people in Serbia.

"The fact that most of these attacks aren't investigated and that the perpetrators are rarely held accountable means they can't be dismissed as isolated incidents," said Stefanovic. "They represent a systemic problem that further stokes violence and emboldens perpetrators to continue attacking marginalized people, without having to fear significant consequences."

The social climate has become decidedly harsher for Serbia's LGBTQ+ community over the last few years, with the community also increasingly the target of right-wing nationalist government.

More recorded attacks than ever before

Da se Zna! is based in an unassuming office on a side street in the center of the Serbian capital. Aside from a lone rainbow-colored nutcracker standing on a shelf, hardly anything indicates the group's purpose: it's the only organization in Serbia to document attacks on queer people — threats, vandalism, physical assault.

"Last year, we counted 110 cases — more than ever before," said Stefanovic. That's due in part to the fact that the NGO is becoming more well-known, and queer people are increasingly ready to report incidents. But dramatic, high-profile cases like the aggression against Alexis Plastik are also happening more and more.

In mid-May, unknown assailants attacked Mornar, a queer bar in Belgrade, with tear gas. At the end of May, a trans woman and her partner were beaten unconscious one night — again, by unidentified attackers.

Many queer people in Serbia are scared of openly showing their identity. In a recent survey by the European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights, some 80% of respondents said they avoided holding the hand of their partner in public.

The latest edition of the Rainbow Map, compiled by the International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association, shows that Serbia has slipped to 29th place in Europe, six spots below the European average. Five years ago, it was in 22nd place.

Support amid threats of violence

The only solution to this stigmatization and violence is education, said Stefanovic. Next to the yearly Pride parade co-organized by Da se Zna!, activists also travel to small towns around the country with a Pride Caravan to send a message: we're here, and we're not going anywhere.

In some of the towns, they're greeted by a handful of supporters holding rainbow flags — and dozens of demonstrators shouting homophobic slogans.

After the group published a list of the planned destinations for this year's caravan, they received several death threats. The event in Pirot, in Serbia's southeast, was called off on short notice in mid-July because police could not guarantee the group's safety. Three journalists covering the event were attacked by the mob.

"These protests show the sad reality for queer people living in a small Serbian town," said Stefanovic. "We try to show the people living in these towns that we know how hard it is — and that we haven't forgotten about them."

Struggle to live openly in a small town

Stefanovic knows exactly how it feels to grow up queer in a small town far from the cosmopolitan city of Belgrade.

"I wanted to be a boy for as long as I can remember. Every night I prayed to God that he would turn me into one," he told DW.

Only as a teenager did Stefanovic learn about other people that felt like him — and that they were known as trans. But this knowledge did nothing to ease his worries.

"Once I realized [who I was,] I felt the weight of everything I would have to go through as a result," he said.

It was only when Stefanovic moved to Belgrade for his studies that he felt free enough to openly live as Matija. He came out as trans, first to several professors at the university, then to friends. Finally, one day, he wrote to his parents, an eight-page letter in which he explained everything that had preoccupied him for years.

Stefanovic then made two life-changing decisions: he began hormone treatment to align his biological sex with his gender identity — and he did so openly. At the time, there were very few people living openly as trans in Serbia, and not much information was available on how to undergo gender-affirming treatment.

"It sounds totally cliche, but I wanted to become the person that I needed in my life when I first exploring my own gender identify," said Stefanovic. He filmed his transition, first putting his videos on YouTube and then on TikTok.

TV interviews followed soon after — and the attention of right-wing groups on Facebook. At first, the hate directed toward Stefanovic seemed unbearable. But he decided to keep going, to stay visible, so that trans people would someday belong.

Stefanovic knows that acceptance is a process, and that people can change their views. His family is a prime example — his conservative father was the first person to consistently use the right pronoun and new name. And last year, both his parents took part in Belgrade's Pride parade for the first time.

"I'm so proud of them," said Stefanovic. "My parents have become my greatest allies."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Europe wildfires rage on, forcing more than 250,000 from homes
entries.summary: From the outskirts of Bordeaux to communities near Madrid, fast-moving wildfires in France and Spain are driving mass evacuations, destroying homes, and claiming lives.
entries.content:
Europe

Europe wildfires rage on, forcing more than 250,000 to flee

Published July 25, 2026last updated July 25, 2026

From the outskirts of Bordeaux to communities near Madrid, fast-moving wildfires in France and Spain are driving mass evacuations, destroying homes, and claiming lives.

As wildfires continue to engulf massive stretches of western France and central Spain, more than 250,000 people have been forced to flee, with flames devouring forests and homes near Bordeaux and Madrid.

Firefighters have said that the blazes, the largest recorded in both countries in recent years, are so massive that they cannot be tackled head on.

Man killed in wildfire near Valencia

The Spanish Interior Ministry said Saturday that a man was killed in a wildfire in the town of Manises, near Valencia.

Local authorities said firefighters managed to bring the blaze in Manises under control but "unfortunately the fire has claimed the life of one person." The body was found in a car in a ravine.

Two French firefighters died earlier this week near Bordeaux and one in Sicily, Italy, which is now also battling blazes.

On France's Atlantic coast, 44,000 people were removed from the Cap Ferret peninsula, many by boat.

Towns near Bordeaux, the famed winemaking town popular with tourists, were evacuated "as a precaution" as strong winds fueled approaching flames.

On Saturday morning, regional authorities further ordered the evacuation of three of the city's western suburbs "to ensure residents' safety."

In all, French authorities say more than 197,000 people have been evacuated in France's western Gironde and Landes departments.

In Spain, the Interior Ministry said 70,000 have been forced to flee.

EU sending firefighting aircraft to France and Spain

Authorities in France say the country's two main blazes were sparked accidentally, however, as summers become drier and hotter the magnitude of such fires has increased exponentially.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who said the government would do everything possible to protect citizens, warned that a wind shift had transformed the Cap Ferret blaze into "a large, self-sustaining fire that is extremely difficult to bring under control."

"It is now moving east, toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area," added Nunez, who pledged, "We are going to reorganize our response so we can fight it from the ground and prevent it from advancing toward Bordeaux."

French President Emmanuel Macron called for European Union assistance on Friday as well as the mobilization of the French army to halt fires that have so far destroyed 22,000 hectares (54,000 acres) of land.   

The European Commission announced that it is sending three firefighting aircraft to France and four to Spain in an effort to gain the upper hand.

This week's fires have injured dozens of firefighters and killed three of them — two in western France and one in Sicily, Italy, which is now also battling blazes.

The Tour de France has been shortened and will be effectively limited to Paris on Sunday because emergency services are needed to deal with wildfires in the country.

Spain declares national emergency

In Spain, the government has declared a national emergency as two of the country's three current fires, all burning near the capital Madrid, merge into one.

Madrid's regional emergency management services said the massive blaze has now reached "its peak and is currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain."

The largest active fire in the region, in Guadalajara province, has already laid waste to some 32,000 hectares.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez visited affected areas west of the capital on Saturday and stressed that the priority was "to save lives," as temperatures in the region topped 37 degrees Celsius (98.6 Fahrenheit).

NASA abandons comms facility amid Spain's summer of fire

The US space agency NASA on Saturday reported that it had been forced to evacuate its Madrid Deep Space Communications Complex (MDSCC), which is located in the region. The facility is one of three worldwide that allow the agency to communicate with spacecraft in distant parts of the galaxy — the others are located in Australia and the US.

"The safety and well being of our personnel is our highest priority and our thoughts are with the families and neighbors who are also experiencing the impact of the wildfires in the surrounding communities," said a statement released by the agency.

Spain, which regularly sees wildfires, has experienced an especially devastating summer. Earlier this month, fires in the south of the country killed 13 people.

Environmental officials say that 1,140 square kilometers (440 square miles) have already been lost to flames this year, more than five times the area burnt throughout the first half of 2025.

Edited by: Kieran Burke and Rana Taha

entries.title: Lenacapavir will slow HIV infections if there's enough of it and it reaches at-risk groups
entries.summary: Lenacapavir is one injection, twice a year. It's a big improvement for people in high-risk groups, currently taking a pill a day against HIV infection. But its long-term impact depends on it reaching those very people.
entries.content:
ScienceGlobal issues

Lenacapavir may slow HIV infections 'but there's not enough'

July 25, 2026

Lenacapavir is one injection, twice a year. It's a big improvement for people in high-risk groups, currently taking a pill a day against HIV infection. But its long-term impact depends on it reaching those very people.

For a healthy young woman in South Africa, the greatest risk of HIV may come from someone she wants to trust, but can't.

She may not know her partner's HIV status, may not always be able to insist they use a condom, and may have little control over whether he has other partners.

There is an option: Daily Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) pills keep antiretroviral drugs in the body at high enough levels to stop HIV before it can establish an infection.

But PrEP only works if she keeps taking the medication. Miss too many doses and drug levels can fall too low to provide sufficient protection.

She may forget, resent having to take a daily pill, or fear that a partner or relative will find the medication, causing stigma. She may also experience side effects from PrEP or struggle to obtain new supplies.

How can lenacapavir help?

Taking medication consistently — known as adherence — is a challenge for people with conditions like hypertension and diabetes. With PrEP, however, the difficulty is even greater.

"You're asking people who are healthy, who don't have any illness, to take a tablet every day," said Salim Abdool Karim, director and co-founder of the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in South Africa. "That's a high bar."

"Repeated studies, including our own, show that patients who start taking PrEP, by month three, about half of them have given it up. By the end of the year, you're left with only a handful that are still taking PrEP," Abdool Karim told DW.

Lenacapavir sharply reduces that daily burden: It requires just one injection every six months.

"That's infinitely easier to do than to remember to take a tablet every day," he said. "For those who receive the injection every six months without fail, it works superbly because adherence is effectively complete."

But lenacapavir is still too expensive in some regions and access is low.

How does lenacapavir last so long in the body?

Most established PrEP drugs block enzymes that allow the virus to reproduce and spread — it uses the enzymes to copy its own genetic material and insert it into a human cell's DNA.

Lenacapavir works completely differently. It is the first PrEP drug to target the capsid, a cone-shaped shell that surrounds the viral genetic material. But the capsid is also essential to the virus' replication process, and therefore a promising target.

"[Lenacapavir] is the most potent molecule we know of against HIV," Wesley Sundquist, a University of Utah biochemist and leading expert on the HIV capsid, told DW.

Sundquist said lenacapavir remains effective over long periods and that it is potent even at low concentrations.

"It sets up a little depot that slowly dissolves," said Sundquist.

Which groups would benefit from lenacapavir?

Abdool Karim pointed to three groups where HIV incidence remains stubbornly high and greater PrEP uptake is urgently needed:

  • Adolescent girls and young women in parts of Africa
  • Younger gay men in the West
  • Vulnerable gay communities in Eastern Europe and Central Asia

In South Africa, a rollout for people at risk began in June 2026, backed by a July 2025 agreement between the drug's developer, Gilead, and a public-private financing organization called the Global Fund.

Gilead agreed to supply lenacapavir at no profit to up to 2 million people over three years.

Earlier, in October 2024, Gilead also agreed to allow the production of cheaper, generic versions of the drug in 120 resource-limited countries, where HIV infection rates are high.

But some countries still lack access to the drug.

Latin American countries excluded from lenacapavir deals

Melissa Scharwey of Doctors Without Borders said some Latin American countries, including Brazil, Mexico, Peru and Argentina have been excluded from recent rollouts of lenacapavir, despite having participated in clinical trials.

Even within eligible countries, vulnerable groups may still be missed, Scharwey told DW.

"There's by far not enough of it," said Scharwey, calling on Gilead to increase supply and sell directly to MSF at an affordable price of around $40 per shot.

The decisive question in driving down HIV, according to University of Washington epidemiologist Monisha Sharma, is whether the drug reaches the people and places where HIV is spreading most rapidly.

"In our modeling of South Africa, Zimbabwe, and western Kenya, providing lenacapavir to approximately 2–4% of the adult population, with targeted uptake among people at greatest risk, averted approximately 12–18% of new infections over ten years," Sharma told DW.

Lenacapavir 'unlikely to eliminate HIV on its own'

"Lenacapavir could substantially accelerate progress toward lowering incidence, but it is unlikely to eliminate HIV transmission on its own," said Sharma.

"This impact is highly dependent on affordable lenacapavir drug prices, efficient distribution channels, and targeted uptake among people with the highest HIV risk," she added.

That final condition is what gives Abdool Karim his greatest concern. Lenacapavir can largely solve the adherence problem for people who receive it. It cannot solve the harder problem confronting HIV specialists: identifying and reaching those in greatest danger.

"The problem is that those at highest risk need to come forward to take the medication. And often those at the highest risk don't see themselves at risk. That's why they're at risk," said Abdool Karim. "If we cannot reach those at highest risk, then we're not going to make a dent in this epidemic in the manner in which we were hoping."

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

entries.title: Tour de France final stage shortened due to wildfires
entries.summary: Security personnel assigned to the race have been redeployed to help contain major blazes near Bordeaux, reducing Sunday's final stage.
entries.content:
July 25, 2026

Security personnel assigned to the race have been redeployed to help contain major blazes near Bordeaux, reducing Sunday's final stage.

Sunday's final stage of the Tour de France will be shorter than planned because security forces have been redirected to help fight wildfires near Bordeaux, organizers and police said Saturday.

"In a spirit of national solidarity with the areas and communities affected, it was decided to adapt the route for the final stage from Thoiry to Paris," the Paris police and the event's organizers said in a joint statement.

Slovenian four-time champion Tadej Pogacar has all but sealed victory in the world-famous cycling race and only needs to finish Saturday's stage to secure a fifth Tour title in seven years.

Final stage shortened to 89 kilometers

The route for Stage 21 has been shortened to 89 kilometers (55 miles), down from the 133 kilometers originally planned.

It was set to begin east of Paris in Thoiry but will now start with two laps on the Champs-Elysees.

Riders will then race the circuit before finishing on the Champs-Elysees as usual.

The team presentation will still be held in Thoiry before riders are taken to Paris by bus.

"The Paris police prefect and the Tour de France director salute the commitment of all the actors mobilized in the fight against the fires and express their full solidarity with the affected populations," the statement said.

Wildfires near Arcachon Bay, near Bordeaux in Gironde, and around Biscarrosse in Landes have destroyed more than 36,000 hectares of forest and forced nearly 200,000 people to evacuate.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Dozens dead after buses collide in eastern Syria
entries.summary: The crash on a route notorious for deadly accidents prompted a large-scale rescue operation.
entries.content:
Syria

Dozens dead after buses collide in eastern Syria

July 25, 2026

The crash on a route notorious for deadly accidents prompted a large-scale rescue operation.

At least 35 people were killed and 30 others were injured when two buses collided in eastern Syria.

The crash happened on Saturday on a highway linking Damascus with Deir al-Zour province.

What else do we know about the crash?

The Interior Ministry said one bus was carrying security personnel, while the other was carrying civilians.

State television footage showed one of the vehicles engulfed in flames after the impact.

Military helicopters were sent to the scene to help evacuate the injured and recover the bodies.

The cause of the crash remains unknown.

The route is widely known as the "road of death" because of its frequent and often deadly accidents.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Germany news: Industry hemorrhaging 15,000 jobs a month
entries.summary: Industry boss Tanja Gönner says the situation is critical but offers opportunity. Meanwhile, politicians head to the Bayreuth Festival and security services warn of racist fight clubs. Follow DW for the latest.
entries.content:

Germany news: Industry hemorrhaging 15,000 jobs a month

Published July 24, 2026last updated July 26, 2026

Industry boss Tanja Gönner says the situation is critical but offers opportunity. Meanwhile, politicians head to the Bayreuth Festival and security services warn of racist fight clubs. Follow DW for the latest.

  • The BDI boss urged innovation in the face of Chinese competition and US tariff burdens

  • Politicians including Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Bavarian State Premiere Markus Söder are expected to attend the opening of this year's Bayreuth Festival, the 150th installment of the annual music festival featuring works by 19th century German composer Richard Wagner

Berlin CSD: 1 dead, several injured after vehicle drives into crowd

At least one person was killed and more than a dozen others were injured after a white van drove into people at a CSD even in Berlin on Saturday night.

The world-famous Pride event was closed early and police launched a manhunt.

Police did not say whether the incident was intentional or not, but Berlin's Mayor Kai Wegner described it as "an attack on our free and open society."

Read DW's full coverage of the fatal vehicle incident at Berlin CSD here.

Skip next section Germany's best gather in Bochum for track and field national championships

Germany's best gather in Bochum for track and field national championships

The country's top athletics stars are gathered in the industrial Ruhr region city of Bochum this weekend for the 2026 German Championships.

The event runs through Sunday evening at the Lohrheide Stadium in the Wattenscheid district in the west of the city.

European champion Julian Weber was back in action in the javelin on Saturday after a lengthy absence with injury. He claimed his sixth German championship with a throw of 82.60 meters, with Nick Thumm his closest challenger on 81.45 meters.

Simon Batz took gold in the men's long jump, 25 centimeters clear of the field with a leap of 8.29 meters.

Later on Saturday, German number 1 Owen Ansah won the 100 meters in a time of 10.00 seconds, just two hundredths shy of his own German record. Ansah claimed the win amid the ongoing scandal over him refusing to submit a sample to the national anti-doping agency earlier this month. Ansah says he has nothing to hide but that the inspector came and demanded a sample outside the agreed hours when he did not have time to comply.

"I wanted to show everyone that I am the fastest German. I wanted to put on a show, and I managed that," he told ZDF public television after the race.

Skip next section Small plane crashes into house, 2 killed

Small plane crashes into house, 2 killed

Two people have died after a light aircraft crashed into the roof of a house in northern Germany on Saturday.

The small plane could be seen embedded in the roof of the small detached house in Ganderkesee, near Bremen. 

Police initially said they had identified one dead person in the plane's wreckage but had not yet been able to remove the body. They were still searching for a second person who was in the aircraft at the time of the crash.

The second body was found later.

Emergency services were first called to the scene at around 11 a.m. local time.

The plane had suddenly lost altitude and crashed for reasons that are not yet known.

The residents of the house were not home at the time of the crash, according to the fire services.

Police said they were not aware of any further injuries.

A help station was set up for local residents who might have witnessed the crash and could be traumatized.

Police also cleared out houses in a 100-meter (roughly 110-yard) radius amid the rescue and recovery efforts. But they stressed this was a precautionary measure and not because of continued danger to the public.

Skip next section CDU's Frei voices sympathy for Merz's slow-motion reshuffle

CDU's Frei voices sympathy for Merz's slow-motion reshuffle

Thorsten Frei has defended Chancellor Friedrich Merz's gradual moves to rearrange government personnel. 

The Cabinet reshuffle was triggered by Jens Spahn's forced resignation.

Frei, Spahn's replacement as the parliamentary floor leader for the CDU/CSU conservatives, told an industry and trade event that he thought the delay was unavoidable.

"Even in top-level politics there is the danger that you can simply get unlucky," Frei said.

He was talking about the apparent delay in replacing Transport Minister Patrick Schnieder.

We know that Schnieder was set for the chop, because he told several party colleagues this in a text that soon leaked out, saying Merz would announce it at yesterday's press conference in Berlin. 

However, seemingly as Schnieder's replacement was not yet lined up, no news of a new transport minister emerged.

More centrist members of the party, like Peter Altmaier — known as a close ally of Angela Merkel, who had a famously poor relationship with her erstwhile rival Merz — had complained online.

Altmaier said he was "upset and angry" about the way Schieder was being treated, describing him as an "experienced professional, hard worker and great person and friend."

Merz is thought to have lined up a 60-year-old replacement for Schnieder, Fritz Güntzler, who at first said he would take the job and then changed his mind shortly before the announcement.

Media reports suggested he felt he lacked the tools to take up the job, with party sources cited as saying "a goalie shouldn't play on the left wing."

Skip next section Right-wing 'active clubs' spreading in Germany, says domestic intelligence agency

Right-wing 'active clubs' spreading in Germany, says domestic intelligence agency

Germany's Federal Agency for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) is warning of the spread of so-called "active clubs" across the country. 

The warning was published on Saturday in Germany's Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper.

The BfV's own website says such clubs, which got their start in the US, have spread to Germany and other European countries over the past several years.

According to the BfV, the clubs target young white males, functioning as a path from online isolation to personal contact.

The fight groups are seen as a gateway to indoctrination into right-wing extremist ideology and are designed to prepare members for what organizers say is a "coming race war."

The BfV says it is actively monitoring the scene and has recorded the founding of a number of such groups across Germany since early 2024.

Authorities say that they have "information on persons with relevant ties to the scene," adding that they have also seen clear ties between active clubs and right-wing extremist parties.

According to the BfV in the southern state of Bavaria, Patrick Schröder of the right-wing extremist party "The Homeland" (Die Heimat, formerly the neo-Nazi NPD) has been instrumental in fashioning a "roadmap" for establishing a broad network of such white supremacist clubs across the country.

Saturday's Süddeutsche article lists 22 such groups in Germany. Although the BfV has warned of the real world threat the groups pose, it is unclear how many actually exist and function as such in real life as opposed to strictly online.

Skip next section BDI boss says Germany shedding 15,000 jobs a month

BDI boss says Germany shedding 15,000 jobs a month

Welcome back to our coverage.

Tanja Gönner, director general of the Federation of German Industries (BDI) described the fact that the country is losing 15,000 each month "critical" while at the same time arguing that it is not too late to turn the situation around.

Speaking with Germany's dpa news agency, Gönner said: "I am convinced that if we do our homework, we will have every opportunity again. Innovation has long been a top priority for many companies."

Urging investment in artificial intelligence and other new technologies, Gönner said "Germany has lost ground in terms of competitiveness," and therefore political and business leaders should ask themselves one thing with each decision they make: "Does it contribute to competitiveness? Does it help companies become more competitive again?"

Gönner stressed that structural weaknesses coupled with US tariff burdens and Chinese competitiveness had put Germany — a former industrial export powerhouse — in its current position, arguing, "we really ought to be heading to the gym to work off the excess weight we've put on over recent years." 

The roughly 100,000 companies represented by the BDI employ over 8 million workers.

Skip next section Foreign Minister Wadephul draws international law and traffic offense analogy in satire show interview

Foreign Minister Wadephul draws international law and traffic offense analogy in satire show interview

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has taken the bold but risky move of appearing in a feature interview on public television's premiere weekly satirical comedy the "heute-show," roughly like the US "Daily Show."

Wadephul speaks at some length to young anchor Fabian Köster in an elevator in a playful interview that's nevertheless focused on entirely serious topics. It spans NATO relations and Donald Trump and Greenland, Russia's war against Ukraine, the low popularity of government he serves in, the war in Iran and Nicolas Maduro's abduction from Venezuela. 

"We're not conducting some kind of foreign policy interview here," Wadephul said at one point with a chuckle after a trickier question, only for Köster to immediately reply "doch!" or roughly "oh, but we are!"

When the topic turned to the US military operation to kidnap Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro, Wadephul was asked whether "international law can rub up against the boundaries of Realpolitik." 

"Yes, if you're honest, yes, that's the case," Wadephul said. "But to be honest, we're familiar with this in the rule of law. If you think of yourself in road traffic, for instance, have you always kept to everything 100%?"

Köster said he liked the analogy but noted that "a stop sign is something slightly different" than the abduction of a head of state.

"In the law it's written that you can't drive faster than 50 km/h in a built-up area, but nevertheless sometimes people drive faster. And it's the same, fundamentally, in international law. And you have to deal with that. The laws are there to provide an orientation, but they are never dogmatically upheld 100%," Wadephul said.

Asked whether it was "embarrassing" for Germany to only speak up against breaches of international law if "the right countries" are offenders, Wadephul said it was important to note that there were gradations of color.

"There are differences," he said. "If you, like [Russian President Vladimir] Putin, have been waging five years of war against Ukraine and killing thousands upon thousands of people — including your own people — or if you took this one step against a person in power in Venezuela, who did not exactly keep to international law himself: There really is a difference."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz had faced criticism amid the US operations in both Venezuela and Iran for comments suggesting the situations were "complex." Wadephul expanded on this saying they were politically complex but perhaps simpler from a purely legal perspective, still without explicitly saying they were breaches of the law.

Skip next section Police puzzle over Regensburg bank attacker hitting cashless branch

Police puzzle over Regensburg bank attacker hitting cashless branch

Investigative police officers are trying to nail down the motive of a 20-year-old suspect who was holed up in a Regensburg bank branch for three hours on Thursday and who is suspected of killing an employee.

He is suspected of attacking and fatally wounding a staff member and of attempted robbery.

But Regensburg criminal police investigator Robert Fuchs said the precise motive remained a mystery given the circumstances.

On the one hand, the man was carrying a note suggesting that he was planning a bank robbery and was trying to secure money. On the other, he had targeted a cashless branch, meaning his chances of any meaningful haul were near zero from the outset.

Investigators said in a press conference on Friday that the suspect had used a kitchen knife with a 12-centimeter by 2-centimeter (roughly 4-inch by 3/4-inch) blade.

The 20-year-old was already subject to a weapons ban after a prior incident of him carrying a knife and an electric shock device without authorization.

Police said there were no indications of psychiatric illness but that relevant tests were ongoing. Special units were able to detain him roughly three hours after the first emergency calls. He did not resist.

The man was also in police custody less than 24 hours prior to the crime, investigators said. They said he had turned himself in, saying that he had thrown a beer bottle at a police officer. Police said they investigated the slightly inebriated man's claim and later released him, saying they had no valid reason to detain him.

Fuchs said that the young man had repeatedly come to authorities' attention for minor infractions over the years. He was also repeatedly reported as missing from a facility caring for children and young people.

Skip next section READ — Merz reshuffles Cabinet in aftermath of Spahn's exit

READ — Merz reshuffles Cabinet in aftermath of Spahn's exit

The other big news of Friday morning, frankly, might not live as long in the memory as Klopp's appointment.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shuffled around some more of his Cabinet posts as he tries to fill the gap left by Jens Spahn's forced resignation amid a surrogacy scandal last week. 

Health Minister Nina Warken is taking up the vacancy running Merz's chancellery after the previous occupant, Thorsten Frei, took up Spahn's job as the parliamentary floor leader for the CDU/CSU group.

Carsten Linnemann will step in for Warken as health minister, and youngster Philipp Amthor will become the junior minister responsible for coordinating with the state governements on behalf of the federal government.

Amthor, still only 33, is best known for a 2020 lobbying scandal that put the brakes on his rapid rise through the party ranks in his late 20s.

Skip next section IN DEPTH — Jürgen Klopp confirmed as new Germany coach

IN DEPTH — Jürgen Klopp confirmed as new Germany coach

In case you missed it this morning, Jürgen Klopp is now officially Germany's men's national team football coach. 

This ends a period of weeks where the deal seemingly needed little more than some dotted i's and crossed t's.

The "Normal One" Klopp takes over from Julian Nagelsmann, who resigned in the aftermath of Germany's disappointing exit on penalties against Paraguay in the World Cup.

DW Sports' Jon Harding looks at a partnership long in the making — with Klopp's name having been linked to the national team job for years already — in this feature story. 

Skip next section Sharp rise in extremist violent crimes in Baden-Württemberg in 2025

Sharp rise in extremist violent crimes in Baden-Württemberg in 2025

The internal intelligence agency, known as the Verfassungsschutz, for the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg has published its annual report for 2025. 

"We all notice that the challenges remain considerable," the president of the state intelligence agency, Beate Bube, said. "The crises of the world are also having an effect here. On top of that there are worrying developments in almost every working area of the Verfassungsschutz."

The report showed rapid increases in violent extremist crime from both the far right, 97 crimes compared to 54 in 2024, and the far left, 49 crimes compared to 34 the previous year.

The number of people classified as far-right extremists hit a new high of 3,790, up from 3,140 in 2024. The number of crimes motivated by far-right ideology dropped marginally, to 2,537 cases.

The number of perceived far-left extremists rose slightly to 2,730, 880 of whom were classed as willing to commit violence. The number of crimes attributed to the far-left scene rose by 80% year-on-year, to 608 cases from 342 in 2024.

The report also noted the growing dangers of hybrid threats, acts of sabotage, online disinformation, and Russian "disposable agents," as well as what it termed the "secular pro-Palestinian extremist spectrum" amid protests in support of Gaza in 2025, differentiating this group from German and Turkish leftists or Islamists.

"2025 has shown us: Extremist threats to our security are becoming more varied, complex and digital," state Interior Minister Manuel Hagel said. "The boundaries between internal and external security, between war and peace are disintegrating. The threats are wholly concrete — and reveal themselves in drone flights over critical infrastructure, in disinformation campaigns and in acts of sabotage."

He said the threats were becoming "more dynamic and subversive," and also noted that they were "reaching ever more young people."

Skip next section VW's Q2 profits dip, boss Blume wants clarity on savings plans by year's end

VW's Q2 profits dip, boss Blume wants clarity on savings plans by year's end

The Volkswagen Group filed its second quarter results on Friday, with profits continuing to dip for the struggling car giant. 

The company logged net profits of €1.54 billion (roughly $1.75 billion) in the second quarter, a 32.9% drop compared to €2.29 billion in the same quarter of 2025.

Although the vagaries of the Trump administration's tariff regime hardly help, most of the company's woes can be traced back to China. 

Sales, particularly of high-value and high-margin models, in the world's second-largest car market are stagnating as China's economic growth slows. And VW is also struggling with intense Chinese competition both on the Chinese market, and increasingly in Europe as well, as Chinese carmakers look to tap new markets amid the domestic slowdown.

Some in the company are calling for more drastic job cuts and factory closures. 

"In a situation where the overall market in China is shrinking by 20% and Chinese competitors are increasing their exports and therefore the competitive pressure in Europe, the currently planned initiatives do not suffice," board member Arno Antlitz said.

CEO Oliver Blume, meanwhile, said a savings program alone would not suffice. He said the priority should be making VW faster, more resilient, more competitive and more innovative. He said they needed to find a way to stay profitable if only selling 8 million vehicles a year, and said he wanted details to be finalized by the end of 2026.

"VW's business model does indeed face pressure in many areas and needs optimization," Blume said, albeit adding that it was also clear that, "a debate about factory closures and historically unprecedented personnel cuts is not the new business model for the VW Group, because that's not a new source of revenue or profits, it brings no technological advantage, creates no competitive products and taps no new markets for our vehicles."

Some initial measures, like reducing the range of products on offer, seeking to streamline production, should be complete this year, Blume said. Larger steps would take time, he added, saying it was unrealistic to expect full factory closures before 2030.

The Volkswagen Group comprises multiple major automakers in Germany and beyond, also including Audi, Porsche, Seat, Skoda, Lamborghini, Bentley and Ducati.

entries.title: Could 'mesh networks' help overcome authoritarians' internet blocks?
entries.summary: In authoritarian countries, the state is often either monitoring online communications or has the ability to shut them down in a political crisis. But there are other ways that activists can keep in touch.
entries.content:
TechnologyGlobal issues

Could 'mesh networks' help overcome state internet blocks?

July 25, 2026

In authoritarian countries, the state is often either monitoring online communications or has the ability to shut them down in a political crisis. But there are other ways that activists can keep in touch.

Iran, January 2026: During some of the country's largest protests in decades, the Iranian government shut down the internet.

US-based internet monitor, IODA — short for Internet Outage Detection and Analysis — registered almost no data traffic at all and US internet infrastructure analyst Doug Madory described it as "one of the largest government-directed communication shutdowns in history."

During that time, the Iranian government killed and arrested thousands of people but to this day, nobody knows exactly how many. Estimates of the death toll have been anywhere between 7,000 and 40,000, though many observers suspect its closer to the higher number. The lack of clarity is partially because the internet blackout meant that communication with the outside world was all but impossible.

The Iranian government's behavior is not unusual. In Russia, Belarus, Myanmar and Sudan, particularly when governments fear resistance, the internet has become a weapon — because those who cannot communicate cannot organize.

Radio-powered networks

One solution for these sorts of communications crises could be what is known as a "LoRa mesh network."

LoRa, which is short for "long range," is based on a simple principle invented for industrial purposes. Small radio modules, also known as LoRa transmitters, have regularly been embedded into physical silicon chips that are used for industrial devices that connect to the internet, things such as smoke alarms, smart water or power meters and environmental sensors — basically any device that requires long battery life and long-range data transmission but only for small amounts of data.

To transmit information, these devices use license-free radio frequencies of the sort available for civilian use, the same frequencies used by weather stations and garage door openers.

To form an internet-free communications network, users first need to purchase a transmitting device that uses LoRa; these can cost anything from about €30 ($35) to €80 ($91). Then users can connect their phone to the device using special software.

The LoRa devices transmit encrypted data packets over a distance of several kilometers. Each device automatically forwards messages to the next one, like a baton being passed through a crowd. If any single device fails, the message finds the next nearby device, via a different route. This means the communications network that is formed can repair itself.

The result of all of the above is what is known as a "LoRa mesh network."

The different transmitting devices are called "nodes" in the network and because there is no central node, there's no way the communications network can be shut down. The radio modules can be kept hidden and powered either by batteries or a small solar panel.

Only smaller messages, no pictures

The major disadvantage of a network like this is that, unlike the ordinary internet, users can only exchange smaller messages, with a maximum size of around 237 bytes, equivalent to a short text message.

On the other hand, the less data transmitted, the longer the distance it can travel, the less power it consumes, and the less likelihood the radio transmission could be tracked.

Two of the best-known platforms that enable this type of communication are Meshtastic and MeshCore, both of which are free to use and open source.

Both place emphasis on data protection. The transmitting devices merely forward messages and cannot read the content. Third parties, including the police or government agencies, cannot intercept the messages either.

MeshCore's motto is "your communications, your keys, your control."

That the concept works, even under extreme conditions, has been demonstrated by users in Ukraine. Meshtastic-UA offers a real-time network map that shows active nodes throughout the country; there are a lot of nodes near the front lines.

MeshCore has a similar map showing the global distribution of nodes. But there are also many other users who conceal their locations.

It's not possible to censor information sent on LoRa mesh networks. When governments halt the internet, they do things like block internet addresses and domains, scrutinize data packets and legally compel providers to cooperate.

For example, Russian security agencies require locally operating telecommunications companies to grant them direct access to communications data. Those who don't comply lose their license. This works mainly if communication takes place over the internet.

That is something that doesn't happen with LoRa mesh networks. The messages travel via radio waves, bypassing firewalls and surveillance systems.

Mesh networks imperfect

There are still risks to this kind of communication, however. For one thing, transmitters can be tracked as encryption protects the content of a message, but not the sender's location. Authorities with the right equipment can triangulate the radio signals, meaning they can physically locate the transmitter to within a certain distance.

Additionally, in some countries, operating unauthorized radio equipment is a criminal offense. In Iran or Russia, being found to be in possession of such devices can have serious legal consequences.

With any other mesh network — such as those that use mobile phones as transmitters — a LoRa mesh network can only work if enough people participate. If there are not enough nodes, then the distance messages can travel is limited. Building up a network like this takes time, something that isn't possible in crisis situations.

It is unclear whether anti-government activists in authoritarian states are using LoRa mesh networks at all. For good reason, anyone taking part in such a network would prefer not to reveal it.

However Ukraine has demonstrated that the concept can work in the real world. The hardware and required software is freely available worldwide and the technology is mature enough that even people without a lot of technical expertise can set it up themselves .

In a world where more and more governments are using the internet as an instrument of power, and where companies such as Apple are increasingly subject to government pressure, what options are left for safe communication? A network of small radio modules could be the answer for some.

This story was originally published in German.
